Logistic Regression: things to remember

  • Logistic regression is used when we have a dichotomous dependent variable because it avoids some of the disadvantages of the linear probability model.

  • Logistic regression coefficients represent the effect of a one unit change in X on the logged odds of Y=1

  • “Logged odds” are not intuitive, so it generally makes more sense to interpret logistic regression models in terms of odds ratios or probabilities.

  • However, converting things to odds ratios or probabilities means we can no longer interpret our results as linear.

The logistic function

In terms of probability, the “slope” will determine how quickly Pr(Y=1) approaches 1 or 0 as X changes.

The logistic function

The intercept has the effect of moving the curve right or left.

Review: Odds ratio interpretation

Option one for interpreting logit coefficients:

  • Exponentiate the model coefficients

  • The exponentiated intercept is the odds of Y = 1 when all variables are zero.

  • The other coefficients become odds ratios: so 2 means “the odds double” and .5 means “the odds are halved”

Review: Predicted probabilities

Option one for interpreting logit results

  • Get the linear prediction for a hypothetical case

  • Use the inverse logit function \(\frac{e^\text{linpred}}{1+e^{\text{linpred}}}\) to convert the linear prediction to a probability.

  • We can calculate the “marginal effects” (the effect on a one unit change in X on the probability of y) at some hypothetical values to give a somewhat more intuitive summary of the relationship between X and Y.

Example model

Data source: NAVCO 1.2 Each row represents a mass movement or campaign where participants demanded fundamental changes to the constitutional order in their country (such as regime change or secession.)

An example model

  • Dependent variable success: did this campaign succeed or fail? (1 = success, 0 = failure)

  • Independent variable 1 violence: did the campaign use mostly violent tactics (1 = violence, 0 = non-violence)

  • Independent variable 2 participation_level: 0 to 10 scale measuring the highest % of population to support the campaign.

An example model

model <- logregC(
  success ~ violence + participation_level,
  data = navco_data, 
  printC = TRUE, # saves formatted table of output
  orci = TRUE # calculates odds ratios/CIs
)

Interpreting the output

  • “Raw” logit coefficient outputs don’t tell us much!

  • Positive values mean positive relationships and negative values mean negative relationships. So the effect of violence is negative and more participation means better changes of success.

  • P-values have the same interpretation: each one represents the probability of seeing a result this extreme if the null is true

Interpreting the odds ratios

Exponentiating the coefficients gives us odds ratios. These should be interpreted as multiplying the odds. So:

  • an odds ratio \(>1\) means a positive effect. (ex: 2 means “the odds double” for each unit increase in x)

  • an odds ratio \(=1\) means “no effect” (because the odds are being multiplied by 1)

  • an odds ratio \(<1\) means a negative effect (ex: .5 means “the odds are cut in half for each unit increase in x)

Interpreting the odds ratios

  • Using violence cuts the odds by .46 (roughly halving them)

  • Each one-unit increase in participation increases the odds of success 1.2 times

Interpreting the odds ratios: % change

It’s a little awkward to speak in terms of cutting something by .46 or 1.2 times, so we can also use the “change in odds” column to interpret this.

  • Using violence is associated with a 53% decrease in the odds of success

  • A one unit increase in participation is associated with a 22% increase in the odds of success.

Interpreting the odds ratios: confidence intervals

Our output also includes confidence intervals. An odds ratio of 1 corresponds to “no effect” instead of 0 here. So we would fail to reject the null if our confidence interval contains 1.

Interpreting the odds ratios: caution

When thinking about odds ratios, keep in mind that the base rate matters.

If the initial odds are very low, then “doubling” them doesn’t mean much:

In many cases, it may be more intuitive to think about logit results in terms of probabilities and marginal effects.

Interpreting probabilities

  1. Start by getting a linear prediction using the same approach we used for a linear model.

\[ \text{linear prediction} = \alpha + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2X_2... \]

\[ \text{linear prediction} = -.938 + (-0.764 \times \text{violence}) + (0.201 \times \text{participation_level}) \]

\[ \text{linear prediction} = -.938 + (-0.764 \times \text{violence}) + (0.201 \times \text{participation_level}) \]

Interpreting probabilities

  1. Plug in values for some hypothetical cases

\[ \text{linear prediction} = -.938 + (-0.764 \times \text{violence}) + (0.201 \times \text{participation_level}) \]

Interpreting probabilities

  1. Convert the linear predictions into probabilities with the inverse logit: \(\frac{e^\text{linpred}}{1+e^{\text{linpred}}}\)

(RCPA has a function for this part)

inverse.logit(-0.134)
inverse.logit(0.067)
inverse.logit(-0.898)
inverse.logit(-0.697)

Interpreting probabilities

Remember that you can also use the predict function to do all the math here:

# run the model and assign it to a variable 
model <- logregC(
  success ~ violence + participation_level,
  data = navco_data
)     
# create a data frame with some hypothetical values of each IV
scenario<-data.frame(
  violence = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
  participation_level = c(4, 5, 4, 5)
  )

# get predictions using the model and the new data
predictions<-predict.glm(model, 
                         newdata=scenario, 
                         type='response')

# putting everything together in a data frame:
scenario$prediction<-predictions

# viewing the result:
scenario

Marginal effects

Interpreting probabilities: marginal effects

  • a marginal effect means the effect of a one unit change in X on the probability of Y=1. But there’s no single marginal effect here!
  • for non-violent movements with participation_level = 4, the marginal effect of a one-unit increase in participation_level is + 5 percentage points
  • for violent movements with participation_level = 4, the marginal effect of a one-unit increase in participation_level is + 4 percentage points

Interpreting probabilities: marginal effects

But this is to be expected: the slope of the logit curve is different depending on where we start (the difference is small here, but could be much larger at more extreme values)

So it only makes sense to speak about “marginal effects” at some specific value of all of the predictors.

Interpreting probabilities: marginal effects

  • Marginal effects at the means (MEM): set all values to their average and then calculate the effect of a one unit change in X

  • Marginal effects at representative values (MER): pick some representative values and calculate the effect of changing x

  • Average marginal effects (AMEs): calculate the average effect if X increased by 1 for every case in the data

Interpreting probabilities: marginal effects

Example: what is the marginal effect of moving from non-violence to violence when participation_level is at its mean?

# get the mean value
avg<-mean(navco_data$participation_level, na.rm=T)
# create the hypothetical cases
scenario <- data.frame(
  violence = c(0, 1),
  participation_level = avg
  )

# get predictions
preds<-predict.glm(model, 
                   newdata=scenario, 
                   type='response')

# combine everything in a data frame
scenario$preds <- preds
# view results
scenario

The marginal effect of violence when participation_level is at its mean is about an -18 percentage point drop in the probability of success:

\(.516 - .332 = .184\)

Interpreting probabilities: marginal effects

Or, we could plot the effect across multiple levels of one or more independent variables:

Code 
# prediction when violence = 0 at each level of participation
nonviol_pred <- predict.glm(
  model, 
  newdata = data.frame(participation_level = 0:10, violence = 0), 
  type = 'response')
# prediction when violence = 1 at each level of participation
viol_pred <- predict.glm( 
  model, 
  newdata = data.frame(participation_level = 0:10, violence = 1) , 
  type = 'response')

# marginal effects of violence 
marginal_fx <-  nonviol_pred - viol_pred

plot(
  0:10,
  marginal_fx ,
  xlab = 'level of public participation',
  ylab = 'marginal effect of violence',
  main = 'Marginal fx of violence on Pr(success)',
  pch = 16
  
)
lines(0:10, marginal_fx)

Interpreting probabilities: marginal effects

Or get the average marginal effect (AME) across all cases:

# model$data will access the dat used to fit the model
# set violence = 0 for all cases and leave everything else at observed values
nonviol_cases<-replace(model$data, 'violence', 0)
# set violence = 1 for all cases and leave everything else at observed values
viol_cases<-replace(model$data, 'violence', 1)

# get predictions for non-violence
nv_preds<-predict.glm(model, newdata=nonviol_cases, type='response')

# get predictions for violence
viol_preds<-predict.glm(model, newdata=viol_cases, type='response')

# calculate the average difference
mean(nv_preds - viol_preds)
[1] 0.1691835

Model fit

How well does our model fit the data?

Model fit

  • In linear regression, we can assess model fit by looking at the distance between the regression line and actual data points.

  • There’s not really an analog in logistic regression: we’re predicting probabilities, but we only ever see a single outcome for each case. So how do we say anything about the quality of a model?

Model fit

Logistic regression models are fitted using maximum likelihood estimation. In essence, we find a set of parameter values (coefficients) that are most likely to have generated the data we see in our sample.

The likelihood function:

\[ \begin{align} \prod^n_{i=1} p_i^{y_i} \times (1-p_i)^{1-y_i}\\ y_i = \text{the actual outcome for an observation}\\ p_i = \text{the predicted outcome for an observation}\\ \prod = \text{the product operator (all these values are multiplied together)} \end{align} \]

Model fit

\[ \begin{align} \prod^n_{i=1} p_i^{y_i} \times (1-p_i)^{1-y_i}\\ y_i = \text{the actual outcome for an observation}\\ p_i = \text{the predicted outcome for an observation}\\ \prod = \text{the product operator (all these values are multiplied together)} \end{align} \]

If \(y_i = 1\) then this simplifies to \(p \times 1\)

If \(y_i = 0\) then this simplifies to \(1-p\)

Model fit

To get the likelihood for this model, we would multiply together everything in the last column.

In short, the likelihood is a measure that will favor models that are very certain about correct guesses and penalize models that are more certain about incorrect guesses.

Model fit

  • We typically work with log likelihoods instead of likelihoods because it simplifies the math (multiplication becomes addition) and because it prevents digit underflow (computers eventually lose precision when trying to track extremely tiny fractions)
# likelihood:
.9 * .8 * .7 * .9 
[1] 0.4536
# log likelihood:
log(.9) + log(.8) + log(.7) + log(.9 )
[1] -0.7905395

Model fit

Then we can compare models based on their total logged likelihoods. A better fitting model will have a higher log likelihood (it will always be negative but better models mean values closer to 0)

Model A

Model B

Model fit

In logistic regression, we can calculate a sort of rough analog to \(R^2\) values (called pseudo-R2) by comparing the log likelihood of a null model (a model with no predictors) to a model that includes our independent variables.

One example is McFadden’s \(R^2\) value:

\[ \text{McFadden } R^2 = \frac{\text{Null Model LL} - \text{Full Model LL}}{\text{Null Model LL}} \]

Higher values indicate a greater improvement over the null model.

Model fit

We can also calculate a p-value to compare models. If we take:

\[ -2 \times (\text{Null Model LL} - \text{Full Model LL}) \]

The resulting value will follow a \(\chi^2\) distribution, so we can use it to calculate a p.value that indicates whether model 2 is a significant improvement over model 1.

Model fit

You can get all of these stats using the logregR2 function:

model <- logregC(
  success ~ violence + participation_level,
  data = navco_data)

logregR2(model)

Code

In case you’re interested, here’s code to access the NAVCO data and run the logit model used in the example.

You can get more information about this data set and what each variable means by navigating to this link and downloading the codebook.

# Run this line to install the dataverse package:
# install.packages(dataverse)

navco <- dataverse::get_dataframe_by_name(
  filename = 'NAVCO 1.2 Updated.tab',
  dataset = 'doi:10.7910/DVN/0UZOTX', 
  server = "dataverse.harvard.edu")

# remove ongoing campaigns
navco<-subset(navco, ONGOING==FALSE)

# rename some variables
navco$success <- navco$SUCCESS
navco$violence <- navco$VIOL

# create 11 equally sized levels of participation
# (the actual % participation is very skewed, which can distort some results,
# so this is just an (imperfect) way to handle that problem)
navco$participation_level <- with(navco, findInterval(
    `PERCENTAGEPOPULARPARTICIPATION`,
    quantile(`PERCENTAGEPOPULARPARTICIPATION`, seq(0,.91, length.out= 11)))-1
  )

# built-in function for logistic regression 
# (fewer features but much faster than logRegC)
model<-glm(success ~ violence + participation_level, 
    data=navco, 
    family='binomial')

# get coefficients and significance values
summary(model)
